summary: Team Aflak from Mazen School, Islamabad, created a 3D lunar rover exploration and base-deployment game for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Players drive a sensor-equipped rover across the Moon to scan terrain slope (steep vs. flat plains), extreme surface and crater temperatures, and radiation levels. Once the rover identifies a location meeting all safety thresholds, players can deploy and spawn their lunar base on-site. Powered by open-source NASA lunar data, the team built and launched the web simulator using Google Gemini, Google AI Studio, GitHub, and Netlify.
details:
Team Aflak developed an interactive 3D lunar rover exploration and base-deployment simulator at Mazen School, Islamabad, for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Built to model the real mission-planning challenges of scouting future Artemis lunar outpost locations, the game puts players behind the wheel of a sensor-equipped lunar rover tasked with surveying the Moon’s surface to locate a safe, habitable zone and deploy a lunar base.

What It Does & How It Works

Team Aflak’s simulator challenges players to drive across an expansive 3D lunar landscape, using live onboard telemetry to evaluate surface and environmental hazards before committing to base construction. It operates through a three-stage scouting and deployment loop:

  1. Free-Roam Lunar Rover Navigation: Players pilot a rover across craters, ridges, and open plains on the Moon, navigating low-gravity terrain while searching for viable outpost sites.
    • Terrain Slope: Distinguishes hazardous steep inclines (where habitats could tip or slide) from flat, stable plains.
    • Surface Temperature: Detects extreme solar heat on exposed terrain versus cryogenic freezing temperatures inside shadowed craters.
    • Radiation Levels: Tracks high-radiation hazard zones versus safe, normal-radiation regions suitable for human crews.
  2. Site Validation & Base Spawning: By cross-referencing live rover sensor readouts, players identify an optimal location that simultaneously meets flat-terrain, moderate-temperature, and safe-radiation thresholds—and then spawn their lunar base directly onto the validated site.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Systems-Thinking in Space Mission Planning: Shows players that selecting a lunar base site requires balancing topography, thermal extremes, and radiation safety simultaneously rather than optimizing for a single metric.
  • Accessible, Browser-Based STEM Learning: Translates planetary science and rover telemetry into an intuitive, hands-on simulation that runs directly in any standard web browser without specialized hardware or downloads.
  • Intended Impact: The project aims to make lunar exploration engineering engaging for young learners and the public, while demonstrating how student innovators can transform open-source NASA lunar datasets into interactive mission-planning tools.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Data & Research: Open-source NASA Space Apps Challenge datasets covering lunar topography, surface temperature extremes, and space radiation environments.
  • AI & Prompt Engineering: Google Gemini to design the rover physics, multi-sensor threshold logic, and modular development prompts.
  • 3D Engine & Frontend Stack: Google AI Studio to build the standalone interactive 3D web application using HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js (WebGL).
  • Version Control & Cloud Hosting: GitHub for source-code management and collaborative iteration, paired with Netlify for instant cloud deployment and live browser access during hackathon demonstrations.
  • Hardware Setup: Developed and tested on student laptops (such as HP ProBooks) and designed to run smoothly across standard laptops, tablets, and classroom computers.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered by the Team

  • Rover-First Telemetry Gameplay: Instead of viewing a static overhead map, Team Aflak placed players directly inside the rover’s scouting workflow—making live sensor interpretation the core mechanic of exploration.
  • Multi-Hazard Trade-Offs: The team specifically factored in how lunar hazards overlap—such as craters offering natural terrain features while presenting steep walls and extreme cold—requiring players to evaluate multiple live telemetry feeds together before deploying a base.
  • Clear Visual Feedback for Decision-Making: Designed clean, real-time sensor readouts so players can immediately distinguish hazardous zones from safe, buildable plains without guesswork.
